title: Super returns slip as Australian equities retreat
full_text:
Superannuation returns are estimated to have fallen in September, with weakness in Australian equities pushing the median balanced accumulation option down 0.4 per cent, according to SuperRatings.
Australian shares fell more than 3 per cent over the month as sticky inflation prompted another cash rate increase from the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA). SuperRatings said the local sharemarket’s underperformance was the main driver of the estimated decline in balanced returns.
US markets were comparatively flat, with strong performers in AI and technology helping to offset weakness across the broader market.
The median growth accumulation option is estimated to have declined 0.5 per cent in September, while the median capital stable option fell an estimated 0.4 per cent.
Despite the monthly losses, balanced and growth accumulation options remained positive for the financial year to 30 September, returning an estimated 0.7 per cent and 0.9 per cent respectively. Capital stable options were flat over the same period.
SuperRatings director Kirby Rappell said Australian shares faced continuing pressure from inflation, economic growth concerns and energy costs.
“Stubborn inflation, concerns around economic growth and elevated energy prices are likely to remain headwinds for Australian shares over the coming months. This is also complicated by the anticipated tightening bias for the RBA. International equities face many of the same pressures, but have been supported by continued investor optimism around AI,” Rappell said.
“However, the sustainability of those gains depends on whether companies involved in the AI ecosystem are able to deliver on the levels of growth anticipated by markets.”
Pension options also recorded estimated losses, with median balanced, growth and capital stable options each declining 0.5 per cent in September.
Over the financial year to date, the median balanced pension option returned an estimated 0.6 per cent and the median growth pension option gained 1.0 per cent. The median capital stable pension option was down 0.1 per cent.
Longer-term accumulation returns remained positive, with the median balanced option returning an estimated 5.9 per cent over one year and 7.4 per cent a year over 10 years. The corresponding returns for the median growth option were 6.8 per cent and 8.7 per cent.
Rappell emphasised the role of diversification and members’ investment time horizons when considering market movements.
“Superannuation remains a long-term investment, and members may have many years, even decades, to ride out the short-term ups and downs of the market,” Rappell said.
“Diversification remains valuable, with super funds investing their members’ money across a wide range of asset classes, sectors, and global regions to help them achieve positive long-term financial outcomes. It’s worth noting that since the bottom of the global financial crisis in 2009, super funds have returned 7.8 per cent per annum to members invested in the median balanced option.
“SuperRatings encourages members who are considering making changes to their investment strategy, or those uncertain whether their strategy aligns with their current circumstances and stage of life, to first speak with their fund or a trusted professional financial adviser.”
author: Adrian Suljanovic
